title: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
summary: How NSA trains sparse attention from scratch with compressed, selected and sliding-window branches and GPU-aligned kernels, and how DeepSeek's DSA picks top-k tokens with a lightning indexer.
outcomes: Explain why post-hoc sparse attention often fails to speed up GQA models or keep quality
Trace NSA's compression, selection and sliding-window branches for one query and count the keys it reads
Compute shared block-importance scores for a GQA group from compressed attention probabilities
Compute NSA's expected decode speedup from its settings and explain why it is capped near the stride d
Compare DSA's lightning indexer and top-k selection with NSA, including training and cost tradeoffs

lessons.title: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints

blocks.md:
Recall from the attention course: a query at position $t$ scores itself against all $t$ earlier keys, takes a softmax, and averages the values. Over a whole sequence of length $L$ that is $O(L^2)$ work. During training and prefill the work is batched into big matrix multiplies, so it is **compute bound**. During decoding, each new token must read the entire KV cache from GPU memory to produce one output, so it is **memory-bandwidth bound**.

The NSA paper (Yuan et al., DeepSeek-AI and Peking University, 2025) cites theoretical estimates that attention accounts for 70 to 80% of total latency when decoding with a 64k-token context.

The hope is that attention is naturally sparse: for a given query, most of the softmax mass lands on a small set of keys. If we could find those keys cheaply and skip the rest, both compute and memory reads would shrink.

Many methods tried this on top of an already trained, fully dense model: evicting KV entries (H2O, SnapKV), selecting KV blocks per query (Quest, InfLLM), or hashing and clustering keys (MagicPIG, ClusterKV). The NSA paper argues these often fail to deliver real speedups, for three reasons.

1. **Phase-restricted sparsity.** Some methods only speed up decoding (H2O) while prefill still pays full cost; others only speed up prefill (MInference). One phase stays dense.
2. **Incompatibility with GQA and MQA.** In grouped-query attention, several query heads share one KV cache. If every head picks its own blocks, the GPU must load the *union* of all picks, so memory reads barely drop.
3. **Not trainable.** Selection is bolted on after pretraining, so the model never learned to work with it. Discrete steps such as k-means or SimHash block gradients, and token-by-token gathers cannot use FlashAttention-style contiguous tiles.

blocks.title: Per-head block selection under GQA loads the union

scenes.caption: Four query heads share one KV cache (one GQA group). A Quest-style method lets each head pick its own top 2 of 8 KV blocks. Each head computes on only 2 blocks.
But the KV cache is shared, so the kernel must fetch every block any head wants: the union is 5 of 8 blocks. Compute fell to 2/8 per head, memory traffic only to 5/8.
NSA's fix: all heads in a group agree on one shared selection. Now the group loads exactly 2 blocks, and every loaded block is used by all 4 heads.

blocks.md:
The trainability problem is just as serious. MagicPIG's authors (cited by NSA) found that the top 20% of attention scores cover only about 70% of the total attention mass, so pruning a dense model after the fact throws away real signal. Specialized structures such as retrieval heads are especially fragile.

The conclusion the NSA authors draw: sparsity must be **native**. The model should be trained with the same sparse attention it will use at inference, and the sparse pattern must be shaped around how GPUs actually move memory.

Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

blocks.question: A model uses GQA with 8 query heads per KV group. A sparse method lets each head choose 4 of 64 KV blocks independently, and the heads mostly disagree. During decoding, roughly what happens to memory traffic per group?
options: It drops to 4/64 of dense, since each head reads 4 blocks
It drops to somewhere up to 32/64 of dense, because the union of the heads' picks must be loaded
It is unchanged, because sparse methods never reduce memory reads
It increases, because sparse methods must read all keys to score them
blocks.explain: Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so the kernel loads the union of their selections: up to 8 x 4 = 32 distinct blocks. Compute per head is 4/64, but decoding is memory bound, so the union is what sets latency. This is exactly why NSA forces one shared selection per group.

blocks.question: Why does NSA insist on applying sparsity during pretraining instead of adding it to a finished dense model?
options: Sparse attention cannot run at inference time without training
Dense models have no attention sparsity to exploit
Post-hoc methods use more KV cache memory than NSA
Training with sparsity makes the model's attention patterns adapt to the selection, and it also makes long-context training itself cheaper
blocks.explain: A dense model's attention spreads mass in ways a fixed selector cannot fully capture (top 20% covers about 70% of mass in MagicPIG's measurements). Training natively lets the model learn patterns that fit the selector, and long-context pretraining and fine-tuning also get faster because the forward and backward passes are sparse.

lessons.title: Three branches: compress, select, and slide

blocks.md: NSA keeps the attention formula but changes *what the query attends to*. For each query $q_t$, it builds a small set of remapped keys and values $\tilde K_t, \tilde V_t$ from the full history, and attends only to those. It builds three such sets, one per **branch**, runs ordinary attention on each, and mixes the three outputs with learned gates.

blocks.tex: o_t^{*}=\sum_{c\in\{\text{cmp},\,\text{slc},\,\text{win}\}} g_t^{c}\cdot \operatorname{Attn}\!\left(q_t,\tilde K_t^{c},\tilde V_t^{c}\right),\qquad N_t=\sum_c \operatorname{size}\!\left[\tilde K_t^{c}\right]\ll t
blocks.caption: Equations 5 and 6 of the NSA paper. Each gate $g_t^c \in [0,1]$ comes from an MLP with a sigmoid on the input features. Sparsity means the total number of remapped keys $N_t$ is far smaller than $t$.

blocks.md: **Compression (cmp).** Slide a window of length $l$ over the keys with stride $d$, and squeeze each block into one key with a small learnable MLP $\varphi$ that includes an intra-block position encoding. Values are compressed the same way. The query sees about $t/d$ coarse summaries of the whole history. The paper uses $d<l$ (blocks overlap) to avoid cutting information at block edges.

blocks.caption: Equation 7: one compressed key per block of $l$ tokens, blocks spaced $d$ apart.

blocks.md:
**Selection (slc).** Coarse summaries lose detail, so NSA also picks the $n$ most important blocks of size $l'$ and attends to *every original token* inside them. How the importance is scored is the next lesson. In the paper's configuration $n=16$ includes 1 fixed initial block and 2 fixed local blocks.

**Sliding window (win).** The last $w$ tokens are always attended in full. The authors found local patterns are learned fastest and can dominate training, so giving them a dedicated branch stops them from shortcutting the other two. Each branch even gets its own independent keys and values.

blocks.title: NSA forward pass for one query

scenes.caption: The cached keys and values feed three branches. Each branch builds its own small key/value set for the current query.
The compression branch attends over about t/d compressed keys. This gives a coarse view of the whole history and, as a by-product, a score for every block.
Those scores pick the top-n blocks, whose raw tokens feed the selection branch (dashed edge). No extra scoring network is needed.
The window branch attends to the last w tokens. Three outputs are combined with sigmoid gates computed from the input features.

blocks.title: What one query sees in a 24-token toy (block size 4)

scenes.caption: Toy settings (simplified): $l=l'=d=4$, $n=4$, $w=4$, query at token 24. The real config is $l=32$, $d=16$, $l'=64$, $n=16$, $w=512$.
Compression: tokens are grouped into 6 blocks of 4 and each block becomes one compressed key c0 to c5. The query attends to these 6 summaries.
Selection: block 0 (initial) and block 5 (local) are always kept; the 2 highest-scoring other blocks (here 1 and 2, computed in the next lesson) are added. All 16 of their raw tokens are attended.
Window: the last 4 tokens are attended through their own branch with their own keys and values. Three outputs are computed and mixed by gates.

blocks.prompt: In the toy above, count the keys the query attends to across all three branches. Is that fewer than the 24 keys of full attention?
blocks.reveal:
No. It is 6 compressed + 16 selected + 4 window = **26** keys, more than the 24 of full attention. NSA's cost is roughly $t/d + nl' + w$, and only the first term grows with context length.

With the paper's settings at $t = 65{,}536$: $\lfloor(65536-32)/16\rfloor = 4094$ compressed + $16 \times 64 = 1024$ selected + $512$ window = **5630** keys, about 8.6% of the context. Native sparse attention only pays off at long context.

blocks.md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

blocks.question: A model must copy the token that appeared 3 positions ago. Which NSA branch is designed to make this easy, and why is it a separate branch?
options: Compression, because it summarizes every token
Selection, because top-n scoring always ranks the most recent block first
Sliding window, because local patterns are learned fastest and a dedicated branch keeps them from shortcutting the long-range branches
None; NSA cannot attend to recent tokens exactly
blocks.explain: The window branch attends to the last $w$ tokens in full. The paper isolates it because local patterns adapt quickly and would otherwise dominate the learning signal of the compression and selection branches.

blocks.question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
blocks.explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

lessons.title: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free

blocks.md: Selection needs a score for every block, and scoring them with a separate network would add cost and need its own training signal. NSA's trick: the compression branch already computed the attention probabilities between $q_t$ and every compressed key. Those probabilities *are* a block-level importance estimate, so they are reused directly.

blocks.caption: Equation 8. When compression and selection blocks coincide, the selection score of block $j$ is simply the compressed attention probability of block $j$.

blocks.md: In the real configuration the blocks do not coincide: compression blocks are $l=32$ tokens with stride $d=16$, and selection blocks are $l'=64$ tokens. The paper's Equation 9 then sums the compressed probabilities of the compression blocks that overlap each selection block (it requires $l \le l'$ and that $d$ divides both $l$ and $l'$). The idea is the same: a selection block is important if the compressed keys covering it got attention.

**GQA sharing.** Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so they must agree on one selection (lesson 1). NSA sums the per-head importance vectors over the $H$ heads of the group, then keeps the top-$n$ blocks of the sum:

blocks.caption: Equations 10 and 11. The selected keys are the concatenation of the raw keys of the blocks in $\mathcal I_t$, so the selection branch sees $n l'$ tokens.

blocks.title: Shared block selection for a 2-head GQA group

scenes.caption: Head 1's compressed attention (softmax of illustrative logits 1.0, 0.2, 2.0, 1.6, 0.1, 1.2). On its own it would pick blocks 2 and 3 as its two free choices.
Head 2 (logits 0.8, 1.7, 1.9, 0.0, 0.3, 1.4) prefers blocks 2 and 1. Picked separately, the group would have to load the union: blocks 1, 2 and 3.
Summed over the group: block 2 = 0.678, block 1 = 0.322, block 3 = 0.287, block 4 = 0.118. The shared scores rank block 2 then block 1 among the free blocks.
Final selection: blocks 0 (initial, forced) and 5 (local, forced) plus the top 2 of the rest, blocks 2 and 1. Head 1 loses its second choice, block 3, but both heads read the same 4 blocks.

blocks.md: Check the numbers: head 1 gives block 1 only 0.059 and block 3 0.239, while head 2 gives block 1 0.263 and block 3 0.048. Summed, block 1 scores 0.322 and block 3 scores 0.287, so block 1 wins the last slot. The selection is a group compromise, which is exactly what makes the memory reads small.

Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

The paper tested the alternatives on a 3B-parameter model: a learnable selector trained with an auxiliary KL loss against pooled attention scores (similar in spirit to SeerAttention), and a parameter-free Quest-style heuristic using the query against the per-block min and max of the keys. Both reached a worse training loss than NSA (Figure 7). The authors also observed that attention in a dense 27B model is blockwise clustered, with neighboring keys getting similar scores, which supports choosing contiguous blocks rather than single tokens.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes letting each of the 16 heads in an NSA GQA group keep its own top-16 blocks, arguing it is more accurate. What is the main cost?
options: The backward pass becomes non-differentiable
Decoding would load the union of up to 256 blocks per group instead of 16, losing most of the memory savings
Compression would no longer work
The window branch would have to grow to compensate
blocks.explain: Heads in a group share KV, so separate selections are loaded as a union. With 16 heads x 16 blocks that can be up to 256 distinct blocks. Summing scores over the group and taking one top-16 keeps reads at 16 blocks while every head uses all of them.

blocks.question: Why does NSA select contiguous blocks of 64 tokens instead of the 1024 individually highest-scoring tokens?
options: Individual tokens cannot be scored
Blocks need less KV cache storage
Token-level selection is not allowed with softmax
Contiguous blocks give coalesced memory loads and Tensor Core tiles, and attention scores tend to be spatially clustered anyway
blocks.explain: GPUs read contiguous memory far faster than scattered indices, and tensor-core matrix multiplies want tiles. The paper also shows attention is blockwise clustered, so blocks lose little. DSA (lesson 5) does select individual tokens, but needs a different kernel design and a separately trained indexer to score them.

lessons.title: Hardware alignment: the kernel and the measured speedups

blocks.md:
FlashAttention (from the GPU basics course) tiles a *contiguous block of queries* into fast on-chip SRAM, then streams blocks of keys and values past it. That works because neighboring queries attend to the same keys. With NSA's selection branch, neighboring queries may want *different* KV blocks, so a query tile would trigger scattered, redundant loads.

The compression and window branches are regular, so they reuse FlashAttention-2 kernels. For the selection branch, NSA writes its own Triton kernel that groups work differently.

1. **Group-centric loading.** For one query position $t$, load all query heads of the GQA group together. They share the same selected blocks.
2. **Shared KV fetching.** The inner loop walks the selected block indices, loading each contiguous KV block of $B_k$ tokens into SRAM once (with $B_k$ dividing $l'$).
3. **Outer loop on the grid.** Every position has about the same number of selected blocks, so the query loop goes to Triton's grid scheduler and work stays balanced across streaming multiprocessors.

blocks.title: Tracing the selection kernel for the toy query
blocks.code:
# selected-attention forward, one GQA group (simplified)
for t in range(T):            # grid: one program per position
    Q = load(q[t, heads])     # all h heads of the group
    blocks = sel_idx[t]       # shared top-n block ids
    m, l, acc = init_state(h) # online softmax per head
    for b in blocks:          # inner loop
        K = load(k[b])        # contiguous block to SRAM
        V = load(v[b])
        S = Q @ K.T * scale   # [h, B_k] on tensor cores
        m, l, acc = update(m, l, acc, S, V)
    store(o[t, heads], acc / l)

scenes.caption: The grid launches one program per query position. Take the toy query at t = 24 from lessons 2 and 3.
Load both heads' queries together (toy group of h = 2; the paper uses 16 heads per group). They will share every KV load.
Read the shared selection computed in lesson 3: blocks 0, 1, 2 and 5.
First selected block: K and V for tokens 1 to 4 are loaded once as a contiguous tile.
One small matrix multiply scores the block for both heads at once, then the online softmax state is updated, just as in FlashAttention.
After blocks 1, 2 and 5 the loop ends: 4 block loads served 2 heads each. Per-head selection would have loaded blocks 0, 1, 2, 3 and 5.

blocks.caption: Arithmetic intensity of one BF16 KV block load (QK and PV multiply-adds over the bytes of K and V), with the paper's $h=16$ heads per group, $d_k=192$, $d_v=128$ and an assumed $B_k=64$ (it cancels). Loading per head would give 1 FLOP per byte; sharing across the group multiplies it by $h$.

blocks.md:
**Training speed.** On an 8-GPU A100 system, against a Triton FlashAttention-2 kernel, NSA's forward pass was 2.1x faster at 8k tokens rising to 9.0x at 64k, and the backward pass 1.1x rising to 6.0x (Figure 6). Speedups grow with length because dense cost grows quadratically while NSA's grows much more slowly.

**Decoding.** Decoding is memory bound, so speed is roughly proportional to how many tokens of KV are read per step: at most $\lfloor (s-l)/d \rfloor$ compressed tokens, $n l'$ selected tokens, and $w$ window tokens, where $s$ is the cached length.

blocks.title: KV tokens read per decoding step (thousands)

scenes.caption: At 8k context: dense reads 8,192 tokens; NSA reads 510 compressed + 1,024 selected + 512 window = 2,046 (the paper's Table 4 lists 2,048). Expected speedup about 4x. Simplified: time taken as proportional to tokens read.
At 32k: dense 32,768, NSA 2,046 + 1,024 + 512 = 3,582. Expected speedup about 9.1x.
At 64k: dense 65,536, NSA 4,094 + 1,024 + 512 = 5,630 (Table 4: 5,632). Expected speedup about 11.6x, matching the paper's headline decode number.

blocks.title: Expected NSA decode speedup versus context length

scenes.caption: Paper settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$). The points are Table 4. The curve keeps rising with context, but bends toward a ceiling.
Doubling the stride to $d=32$ halves the compressed tokens and raises the ceiling to 32, at the cost of coarser summaries.
Selecting more blocks ($n=32$) lowers the speedup at moderate lengths, but barely matters at 1M tokens, where compressed tokens dominate.

blocks.prompt: With the paper's settings, will NSA's decode speedup keep growing without bound as the context reaches 1M tokens?
blocks.reveal: No. At $s = 1{,}048{,}576$ NSA reads 65,534 compressed + 1,024 + 512 = 67,070 tokens, a speedup of about **15.6x**. Because compressed tokens grow as $s/d$, the speedup can never exceed $d = 16$. At very long contexts the compression branch, not selection, is the cost to attack.

blocks.md: **What it bought in quality.** The paper pretrains a 27B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (3B active, 30 layers, GQA with 4 groups and 64 heads) with NSA and with full attention. NSA averaged 0.456 versus 0.443 on nine general benchmarks, 0.469 versus 0.437 on LongBench, retrieved perfectly in a 64k needle-in-a-haystack test, and after distillation on reasoning traces scored 0.121 versus 0.046 on AIME 24 with an 8k generation limit. These are one paper's results at one scale; treat them as evidence that native sparsity need not cost quality, not as a guarantee.

blocks.question: Why does NSA's selection kernel loop over GQA groups at each query position, instead of tiling a block of consecutive queries like FlashAttention?
options: Consecutive queries can select different KV blocks, so a query tile would cause scattered, redundant loads, while heads of one group share exactly the same blocks
Triton cannot tile over the query dimension
It reduces the number of compressed tokens
It makes the selection differentiable
blocks.explain: Within a group, every head reads the same selected blocks, so each contiguous block load is reused h times. Consecutive positions have no such guarantee, so tiling them would not share loads.

blocks.question: At 64k context NSA's backward speedup (6.0x) is lower than its forward speedup (9.0x) and its expected decode speedup (11.6x). Which explanation fits the mechanism?
options: NSA disables sparsity in the backward pass
Decoding uses a larger window
Decoding is memory bound, so its speedup tracks the ratio of tokens read, while training passes are compute bound and include the dense-kernel compression and window branches plus extra gradient work
The forward pass skips the compression branch
blocks.explain: Decode latency is set by bytes read, so it follows the 65,536 / 5,630 ratio. The paper does not break down the training gap, but forward and backward are compute bound, include all three branches, and the backward pass adds gradient work for Q, K and V, so the achieved speedup is smaller than the pure read ratio.

lessons.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens

blocks.md:
DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) is the sparse attention used in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and DeepSeek-V3.2. According to the V3.2 paper, it is the *only* architectural change from DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus, and it was added by continued training of that dense checkpoint rather than by pretraining from scratch.

DSA keeps NSA's goal and its key systems lesson (all query heads must share one selection) but drops the three-branch design. Instead it uses two parts: a cheap **lightning indexer** that scores every past token, and a **top-k selector** that keeps the $k$ best *individual tokens* for the main attention.

blocks.caption: Equations 1 and 2 of the DeepSeek-V3.2 paper. The query token gives $H^I$ indexer queries and per-head weights; each past token gives one indexer key. ReLU was chosen for throughput.

blocks.title: A toy lightning indexer: 2 heads, 6 past tokens, k = 2

scenes.caption: Head 1 (query 1.0, 0.5, -0.5) dotted with six 3-dim indexer keys, then ReLU. Negative matches become exactly 0, so they cannot help a token.
Head 2 (query -0.5, 1.0, 0.5) likes different tokens: 3, 5 and 6. A dense softmax head would mix everything; here each head just votes.
Weighted sum with per-token head weights 0.7 and 0.3 (they come from the query token too). Index scores: 0.175, 0.91, 0.36, 0.49, 0.715, 0.135.
Top-k with k = 2 keeps tokens 2 and 5. Only their key-value entries go into the main attention. In DeepSeek-V3.2, k = 2048 out of up to 128K tokens.

blocks.md: In the released configuration the indexer has 64 heads of dimension 128, runs in FP8, and keeps an extra 128-dimension FP8 key per token per layer; top-k is 2048. The main attention is Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA, from DeepSeek-V2) run in its MQA mode, where one compressed latent KV entry per token is shared by all 128 query heads. That sharing is the same requirement NSA identified: one selection per KV group, so every loaded entry serves every head.

blocks.title: DSA inside one DeepSeek-V3.2 attention layer

nodes.label:
Indexer key cache
128-d FP8 per token

Index scores
I(t, s) for all s

scenes.caption: Each new token writes two things: its MLA latent KV entry and a small FP8 indexer key. Nothing is evicted; the full history stays cached.
The indexer scores the current query against every cached indexer key. This is still O(L) per query, but with few, small, FP8 heads.
Top-k picks 2048 token positions and gathers only their latent entries. The expensive 128-head attention runs on those 2048 entries, so its cost per query stops growing with L.

blocks.md: **Training the indexer.** Top-k is not differentiable, so DSA gives the indexer its own loss. In a **dense warm-up** (1000 steps of 16 sequences of 128K tokens, about 2.1B tokens, learning rate $10^{-3}$) the main model is frozen and still attends densely. For each query, the main attention probabilities are summed over heads and L1-normalized into a target $p_{t,:}$, and the indexer learns to match it.

blocks.caption: Equation 3. In the later sparse stage the same KL loss is computed only over the selected set $S_t$.

blocks.md: Then a **sparse training** stage turns on top-2048 selection and trains everything for 15,000 steps of 480 sequences of 128K tokens (about 943.7B tokens, learning rate $7.3\times10^{-6}$). The indexer's input is detached: the indexer learns only from its KL loss, and the main model only from the language modeling loss. Post-training uses the same sparse attention.

blocks.title: Attention multiply-adds per query: dense MLA vs DSA

scenes.caption: Simplified count from the released config: 139,264 MACs per attended key for the main attention (128 heads, 576-d scores, 512-d values) versus 8,192 for the indexer (64 x 128). Ignores FP8 speed and all non-attention layers.

At L = 128K: dense is about 18,254M MACs, DSA about 1,359M, roughly 13.4x less. Below about 2K tokens DSA is no cheaper. For short prefills DeepSeek instead runs a masked MHA mode that simulates DSA, which it reports is more efficient there.
Raising k to 8192 shifts the crossover right and shrinks the long-context gain. The indexer term (x times 8,192) is the floor that no choice of k removes.

blocks.md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

**NSA versus DSA in one view.**

- **Granularity:** NSA selects blocks of 64 tokens; DSA selects individual tokens.
- **Scoring:** NSA reuses the compression branch's attention; DSA trains a separate FP8 indexer with a KL loss.
- **Coverage:** NSA adds compressed and window branches for global and local context; DSA relies on top-k alone.
- **Adoption path:** NSA was pretrained from scratch; DSA was retrofitted to a dense checkpoint by continued training.

A real-world reminder that details matter: on 2025-11-17 DeepSeek noted that earlier inference demo code applied RoPE in the indexer with the wrong (interleaved) layout, which could degrade outputs.

blocks.question: During DSA's dense warm-up, what is the indexer trained to predict?
options: The next token, using the language modeling loss
Which tokens NSA's compression branch would select
The main attention distribution for each query, summed over heads and L1-normalized, via a KL loss
A binary label for whether each token is in the top 2048
blocks.explain: The target $p_{t,:}$ is the dense main attention summed over heads and normalized. The indexer's softmax is pulled toward it with KL divergence while the main model is frozen, so the indexer learns which tokens the model actually attends to before sparsity is switched on.

blocks.question: Serving cost per token for a DSA model is measured at positions 1K, 32K and 128K. What pattern does the mechanism predict for the attention part?
options: Constant at all positions, since top-k is fixed
Close to dense at 1K, then growing much more slowly than dense, because only the cheap indexer term scales with position
Lower than dense at 1K and identical at 128K
Growing faster than dense because of the indexer
blocks.explain: Below $k$ tokens DSA attends to everything and adds indexer work, so it is no cheaper. Beyond that, the main attention is capped at 2048 entries and only the indexer (about 17x fewer MACs per key in this count) keeps growing with position.

blocks.question: You want sparse attention for a model that will serve 1M-token contexts. Which statement is the best reading of the two designs?
options: NSA's decode speedup grows without limit, so it is strictly better
DSA needs no extra memory per token
Both remove the need to store the full KV cache
Both have a linearly growing per-query term (NSA's compressed tokens, DSA's indexer), so at extreme lengths the cheap scoring path becomes the bottleneck to optimize
blocks.explain: NSA reads about $s/d$ compressed tokens per step, capping its speedup near $d$. DSA's indexer scores all $L$ cached tokens. In both, the scoring or summarizing path scales with context, and both keep the full KV cache.
